President, excellencies, executive director, distinguished delegates. Today is a particularly meaningful occasion for Eritrea. As UNICEF celebrates its 80th anniversary, Eritrea is commemorating 50 years since the establishment of Beit Timotessora, affectionately known as Zero School. Established in 1976 by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front, in the midst of the bitter war for independence, the Zero School was created to ensure that Eritrean children would not become victims of the war around them. They were to be protected, nurtured, and educated despite the extraordinary circumstances in which they were growing up. It embodied a profound provision, a people fighting for its future must protect and prepare the children who will inherit the future. That commitment continued with independence. Among the first international conventions Eritrea signed was the Convention on the Rights of the Child, firmly anchoring the rights and well being of children in the country in the country's national journey. Since independence, Eritrea has made important progress in advancing the survival, health, education, and well-being of its children. Child mortality has declined significantly, while immunization and access to essential health services have expanded. Eritrea has also made progress in expanding access to education and strengthening systems that reach children and families, including in remote communities. These achievements reflect not only the efforts of the government, but also the contribution of families, communities, schools, health workers, and partners, a whole of society commitment to ensure that children survive, are protected and nurtured, receive an education, and have the opportunity to develop to their full potential. UNICEF has been an important partner in this journey. Its partnership with Eritrea dates from the early years of independence, supporting the country's efforts to address the needs of children and families emerging from war. The new country program represents yet another chapter of this partnership. The CPD recognizes that progress brings responsibilities. In education, the focus is increasingly on quality learning and the foundations laid in early childhood. Eritrea is investing in this next change, including the training of 7,000 pre-primary teachers and plans to establish kindergarten centers in nearly 2,000 communities. This is precisely where the whole of society approach matters. Education and protection began long before a child enters classroom and extend far beyond it. Families, communities, teachers, health workers, government institutions, and partners all have a role in creating an environment in which children are safe, healthy, supported, and able to learn. The CPD was developed through a participatory process with Eritrean institutions and stakeholders, grounded in evidence and aligned with Eritrea's national priorities, including Vision 2030 and the forthcoming National Development Plan 2027 to 2031. It builds on national systems and community-based approaches, strengthening what already exists. As we move into implementation, Eritrea looks to UNICEF to continue walking with us in this effort, supporting and strengthening of national capacities and systems, expanding quality early childhood education, improving foundational learning, and reinforcing integrated child protection, particularly for children and communities that remain underserved. 50 years ago, the Zeros School demonstrated this commitment under the most difficult circumstances. Today, we carry it forward through our institutions and communities and partnerships. The children protected and educated during the liberation struggle became the generation that built an independent Eritrea. Our responsibility now is to prepare the next generation to build its future. Eritrea, therefore, welcomes the endorsement of the country program. document and looks forward to a stronger, deeper and results-oriented partnership with UNICEF, grounded in national ownership, mutual respect and a shared commitment to every child. As UNICEF marks 80 years and Eritrea marks 50 years since the zero school, these anniversaries remind us that protecting children is protecting the future, educating children is building the future and building that future is a responsibility we all share. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished Permanent Representative of Eritrea. I now give the floor to the distinguished delegate of Eswatini. You have the floor.

Thank you, Madam President, Madam Executive Director, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. This recognizes that what we do in early years in areas such as survival, health, nutrition, and early childhood development has a direct bearing on children's ability to remain in school, access health and protection services, develop the skills they need, and make a successful transition into adulthood. Eswatini also welcomes the program's focus on system strengthening, improving sustainable financing, using data and evidence, and ensuring equitable last mile service delivery. We value the recognition of national and community structures, including local governance and community institutions, as important partners in reaching vulnerable children and families. This will be essential to ensure that the progress made through the program can be sustained beyond the program cycle. We also underscore the importance of ensuring that system strengthening translates into measurable improvements in the lives of children. This is particularly important for children living in rural areas and underserved communities, children with disabilities, and children experiencing poverty and other forms of vulnerability. As Swaziland looks forward to work closely with UNICEF and our development partners in implementing this program, we remain committed to ensuring that our collective efforts and investments lead to tangible and sustainable results for every child. Eswatini supports the country program document for 2027-2030 and looks forward to its successful implementation. I thank you.

Thank you, Madam President. At the outset, I wish to express our sincere appreciation to UNICEF for its longstanding and effective partnership. For decades, this partnership has supported our national efforts to improve health, education, protection, and well-being of our children. The new country program document for Tajikistan for 2027-2030 comes at an important moment. Children represent around 40% of our population and almost two-thirds of Tajikistan population is under the age of 30. This is both a responsibility and a tremendous opportunity. As UNICEF's Generation 2050 analysis rightly highlights, Sustained investment in children and young people can help Tajikistan turn its demographic potential into demographic dividend. It continues through quality and inclusive education, and it must prepare adolescents and young people for the future. We particularly welcome the focus on digital green and transferable skills, stronger school to work transitions, and closer links with the labor market needs. Protecting children therefore requires stronger preparedness, early warning, and resilient health, education, and social protection systems. Madam President, this country program document is nationally owned. It was developed through close consultations with our ministries and institutions and reflects the development priorities of Tajikistan. We therefore kindly ask the Executive Board to approve Tajikistan's CPD today. I wish to express our particular appreciation to Mr. Artur Vardzishvili. former UNICEF representative in Tajikistan for his leadership, dedication and tireless work in Tajikistan. Ultimately, the success of this program will be measured not by document, but by results in the lives of children. The government of Tajikistan remains fully committed to working with UNICEF to achieve those results for every child everywhere in Tajikistan. I thank you, Madam President.

Madam President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, colleagues, First of all, let me say my sincere thanks to the government of Albania and Tajikistan for their strong partnership throughout the development of their country program documents. In Europe and Central Asia, nutrition is no longer only a question of health. It's a question of equity, resilience, and human capital. Regional nutrition agenda is complex. In parts of Central Asia, children still suffer from stunting, wasting, and anemia, while across many countries, overweight and obesity are increasing. These challenges are manifestation of the same underlying question, whether children and families have the condition they need to survive, grow, learn, and thrive. Poor nutrition affects development and learning today, but it also shapes the productivity, cohesion, and resilience of societies tomorrow. The experience of our region points to one clear lesson. We will not solve malnutrition by scaling isolated intervention. Together with governments, WHO, the EU, and other partners, We have been helping countries move towards a system-based approach to child health and nutrition. Our work includes strengthening breastfeeding support, advancing healthier schools, nutrition, strengthening nutrition financing, and generating the evidence needed to inform policy and investment. The new country programs put this approach into practice. In Albania, for example, addressing nutrition is envisaged by strengthening the provision of integrated services through implementation of a European child guarantee. In Tajikistan, nutrition is a prominent national priority, and UNICEF supports the government to strengthen nutrition governance, financing, and regulatory frameworks. improve prevention and management of wasting, promote breastfeeding and better complementary feeding practices, and create healthier food environments in and around schools. These efforts will be embedded in the wider system that supports children and families throughout the life course. Protecting investments in children is one of the smartest decisions. that governments can make in their future human capital. That's why the next phase of our work must be moving from evidence to policy, from policy to financing, and from financing to implementation at scale. Thank you, Madam President. Back to you.

I thank Mr. Begbeder for his remarks. Thank you, Madam President. I have the honor to deliver this intervention on behalf of Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Grenada, Guyana, St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, as well as my own delegation, Jamaica, on the UNICEF multi-country program document for the English and Dutch-speaking Caribbean countries for the period 2027 to 2031. We express our appreciation to UNICEF for its continued partnership with our governments as we remain committed to ensuring that every child has the opportunity to survive, thrive, and reach their full potential. We are pleased to support the adoption of this MCPD and the consultative process through which it has been developed and its alignment to key frameworks, including the ABAS as well as our respective national development plans. We also welcome the program's three areas of focus, strengthening equitable access to resilient social systems, child protection systems, and the integration and shock responsiveness of social protection and other services. These priorities are in line with those of our respective countries. We recognize that investment in the early years, primary health care, nutrition, mental health, and psychosocial support, early childhood development, and foundational learning are essential to the holistic growth and development of the child. In conjunction with this, education must also prepare children to meet the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead of them, equipping them with the skills, resilience, and ability to achieve their highest potential and to adapt to an ever-changing environment. We therefore encourage UNICEF to enhance its support for strengthened, resilient, and inclusive education systems to ensure that all children, including children with disabilities and children living in vulnerable situations, are not left behind. Madam President, while our respective countries have made significant progress in advancing children's rights and improving their social outcomes, our efforts have been stymied by shocks, including natural disasters, which continue to exacerbate the vulnerabilities of small island developing states. For the Caribbean, therefore, resilience is not an abstract concept. It is a prerequisite for sustainable development. Our experience on the front line of the planetary polycrisis has long demonstrated how suddenly, but with far reaching impacts, crises affect household incomes, food security, education, and access to essential services, particularly for children. To this end, it is imperative that social protection systems have the ability to quickly respond while protecting the investments already made in our children. We therefore welcome the program's recognition of the interconnected challenges impacting the lives of children, its focus on strengthening existing systems, and its emphasis on evidence-based shock-responsive social protection systems rather than relying primarily on stand-alone interventions. Madam President, each of our nations carries its own unique realities, challenges, and aspirations. And while our region cannot be fitted into a single mold or collective objective, it's to ensure that every child can grow up in an environment where their dignity, safety, and rights are respected. For more than half a century, Caribbean governments and their people have practiced and expanded regional cooperation, particularly through CARICOM, and we continue to learn from each other. Our experiences are testament to what we can achieve with greater impact when we share evidence, technical expertise, innovations, and approaches that have demonstrated meaningful results. At the same time, the regional approach of the MCPD must preserve national ownership. Working with stakeholders in the region, UNICEF must ensure that regional solutions remain sufficiently flexible to respond to national priorities while enabling countries to benefit from shared learning. The Caribbean Reference Group provides an important mechanism for maintaining the necessary dialogue and ensuring that governments remain at the center of implementation. Our own commitment must be met with strong partnerships for the success of this program. Our respective governments value UNICEF's collaboration with CARICOM, the United Nations system, international financial institutions, and other development partners. We encourage these partnerships to be well-coordinated around national priorities, and to reduce fragmentation in development assistance. Finally, Madam President, the 12 participating countries in this program are united by the shared conviction that every child in the Caribbean should have the opportunity to grow up healthy, safe, and educated. Every child should also be empowered to realize their full potential and positively shape the future for our societies. The multi-country program document provides us with an opportunity to translate that conviction into collective action, And so, on behalf of the 12 participating countries, we reaffirm our commitment to working with UNICEF and all partners to implement the program. And in this regard, kindly invite the adoption of the multi-country program document by the executive board. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Jamaica for her presentation. And I give the floor to the distinguished delegate of Guyana. You have the floor.

Thank you, Madam President. Allow me to convey Guyana's appreciation to the members of the Executive Board for the important work that you continue to do in implementing UNICEF's mandate. Guyana aligns with the joint statement delivered by the representative of Jamaica. We join in thanking UNICEF for the comprehensive multi-country program document 2027 to 2031, and for UNICEF's continued valuable support and close collaboration with Guyana. Third, the program supports the generation and dissemination of evidence tools and global goods that strengthen program quality, inform decision making, and reinforce accountability. And fourth, it leverages strategic partnership to accelerate results for children. These include partnership with international financial institution, regional institution such as the African Union and the Africa Center for Disease Control and Prevention, mechanism such as the Child Nutrition Fund, and partners across the United Nations development system. Through this function, the Global and Regional Program contributes directly to the achievement of the five impact results of the strategic plan and three of its accelerator. We all know that inequities affecting children exist in every country, and the executive board has already recognized UNICEF engagement with high-income country as part of its universal child rights mandate. In decision 2016-11, the board invited UNICEF to apply the most appropriate modality for such engagement, including through the global and regional program. This global and regional program provides a flexible and efficient governance framework to set up this engagement.
